Cost-Optimal LLM Routing with Limited User Feedback under User Satisfaction Guarantees

Herbert Woisetschläger Affiliation: Technical University of Munich Affiliation: Germany Email: h.woisetschlaeger@tum.de    Arastun Mammadli Affiliation: University of Exeter Affiliation: United Kingdom Email: am2169@exeter.ac.uk    Ryan Zhang Affiliation: Horace Greeley High School Affiliation: United States Email: ryzhangofficial@gmail.com    Shiqiang Wang Affiliation: University of Exeter Affiliation: United Kingdom Email: s.wang9@exeter.ac.uk
Abstract

Inference costs for large language model (LLM) applications are rapidly growing, driven by surging demand and rising infrastructure cost. Users expect high-quality responses, and in commercial settings this is formally codified in Service Level Agreements (SLAs), creating a fundamental tension between cost and quality. Recent progress on cost-aware LLM request routing has shown potential to resolve this tension, but existing approaches rely on complete feedback signals, offline training, extensive per-workload tuning, and most lack SLA guarantees or inference-time adaptivity. We introduce SLARouter, an online routing algorithm that learns a cost-optimal policy from the sparse, one-sided user feedback available in production systems. SLARouter provides theoretical guarantees for both cost optimality and strict SLA compliance. Experiments across a wide range of LLM benchmarks show that SLARouter satisfies SLA constraints without the need for per-benchmark tuning, reducing operating cost by up to 2.2×2.2\times over existing baselines.

   

1 Introduction

The rapid proliferation of open-weight large language models (LLMs) [33, 15, 12, 18], alongside a growing array of API-based offerings, has left both end users and inference service providers facing an increasingly intractable model selection problem. Compounding this challenge is the fragmented benchmarking landscape. Results are often measured on incomparable tasks under inconsistent conditions, making it difficult to determine which model is best suited for a given workload [19]. This leaves practitioners resorting to educated guessing or expensive trial-and-error.

Against this backdrop, LLM routing, i.e., the problem of dynamically selecting an appropriate model for each incoming request, has emerged as a popular technique to improve user satisfaction and reduce inference costs [21, 5, 29, 2, 14]. Instead of committing to a single model, routing frameworks maintain a model zoo and dispatch each request to whichever model best balances quality and cost for that particular query. As model families often span parameter counts from under a billion to over a hundred billion, the cost difference between the smallest and largest model in a zoo can easily exceed an order of magnitude [26], making intelligent routing essential for sustainable operations.

Cost efficiency is especially pressing as LLMs are increasingly deployed in a wide range of applications, where sequences of model calls compound energy expenditure. Emerging AI regulation, such as Article 95 of the EU AI Act [9], further mandates energy monitoring and compliance with sustainable computing best practices. Although there are existing studies on cost-aware routing and first steps towards cost-optimal routing, the following core challenges still remain.

The Need for Formal Service-Level Guarantees. In commercial deployments, cost savings alone are insufficient. Providers and their customers typically codify quality requirements in Service Level Agreements (SLAs). For LLM inference, an SLA might specify a certain task success rate for an AI model over time. Early routing work [21, 10, 1, 4] demonstrated that cost-aware routing between a strong and a weak model is practically effective, but do not provide formal guarantees that the routed system will meet a prescribed quality threshold. More recent efforts have begun to close this gap by introducing minimax rate-optimal guarantees in a two-model setting [28] or formal SLA compliance to larger model zoos [3, 32], albeit most without adaptation at inference time. Fully online methods that continuously update their routing policy as requests arrive remain sparse, especially those that simultaneously provide formal SLA satisfaction guarantees.

The Feedback Bottleneck. A practical obstacle in virtually all existing routing approaches is that they assume the availability of reliable, timely, and complete quality signals. In real-world systems, however, explicit user feedback is sparse. For example, fewer than 5% of requests may receive any signal [11, 17]. When the feedback arrives, it is usually one-sided, i.e., it pertains to exactly one model response. So, the performance of all other models remains unknown. Without addressing this feedback bottleneck, even a theoretically sound routing policy will degrade in practice. We therefore need a routing framework that adapts to user preferences and workload shifts over time based on one-sided observational feedback while providing SLA guarantees.

Research Question. Can we build an LLM router that provides formal SLA guarantees and operates cost-optimally, relying only on sparse one-sided observational feedback available in practice?

Contributions. We introduce SLARouter, a practical and scalable LLM routing algorithm that synthesizes the lessons of prior work into a unified framework capable of operating under production-realistic conditions. SLARouter makes the following novel contributions:

  • •

    Online routing from sparse one-sided observational feedback. SLARouter is an adaptive routing algorithm that learns a cost-optimal routing policy from one-sided and sparse user feedback as it is typically available in production systems. We show that SLARouter is up to 2.2×2.2\times cheaper compared to existing cost-aware routing techniques while providing on par routing performance. While our algorithm also proves to be effective in systems with low user feedback rates, we extend our routing system with an LLM-based judge mechanism [34] to ensure smooth predictor training.

  • •

    Formal SLA guarantees under observational data. We provide theoretical guarantees for cost-optimality under one-sided sparse user feedback while maintaining a required user satisfaction rate over time. Our approach is based on a novel extension to the Lyapunov drift-plus-penalty framework [20]. With our performance analysis, we demonstrate that we can effectively learn from observational data and achieve virtual queue stability in settings with highly sparse feedback rates.

Related Work. Table 1 compares SLARouter to existing LLM routing algorithms. Cost-aware routers such as RouteLLM [21], Hybrid LLM [10], AutoMix [1], and FrugalGPT [4] reduce inference expenditure effectively but offer no formal quality guarantees. CARROT [28] introduces rate-optimal guarantees but does not adapt online. PROTEUS [3] scales SLA compliance to larger model zoos but requires offline training, limiting adaptation to distributional shifts. MESS+ [32] combines online adaptation with formal SLA guarantees, but assumes complete, balanced, and timely feedback for all candidates that is rarely satisfied in production. Causal LLM Routing [30] is the only prior method that learns from observational data, but does not support online adaptation or SLA guarantees. SLARouter is the first to satisfy all five criteria, specifically, cost-awareness, formal SLA guarantees, fully online operation, and learning from the one-sided sparse feedback available in real systems.

2 SLARouter: Practical and Scalable LLM Request Routing with Service Level Guarantees based on Observational Data

2.1 Problem Formulation

We consider a model zoo of MM LLMs, indexed by m∈{1,…,M}m\in\{1,\ldots,M\}, that serve incoming user requests t∈{1,…,T}t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}. For each request, our goal is to select a model that minimizes inference cost while guaranteeing that a minimum fraction α\alpha of requests receive a satisfactory response over time.

Inference Cost (Objective). Each model mm incurs an inference cost Cm,tC_{m,t} per request tt, e.g., energy consumption in megajoules or monetary API cost. Model families routinely span orders of magnitude in cost, so routing intelligently instead of defaulting to the largest model can yield substantial savings.

Service Level Agreement (Constraint). In our SLA, we define α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) as the minimum required user satisfaction rate over time. Violating this threshold is typically associated with contractual penalties, making strict compliance non-negotiable. In practice, α\alpha should be set slightly above the contractually agreed threshold to absorb estimation noise and provide a compliance safety margin.

Control Problem. Combining objective and constraint, we aim to solve:

min{ym,t:∀t,m}\displaystyle\textstyle\min_{\{y_{m,t}:\forall t,m\}}\quad 1T​∑t=1T∑m=1M𝔼⁡[ym,t​Cm,t],\displaystyle\textstyle\frac{1}{T}\sum\nolimits_{t=1}^{T}\sum\nolimits_{m=1}^{M}\mathbb{E}\left[y_{m,t}C_{m,t}\right], (1a)
s.t. 1T​∑t=1T∑m=1M𝔼⁡[ym,t​sm,t]≥α,\displaystyle\textstyle\frac{1}{T}\sum\nolimits_{t=1}^{T}\sum\nolimits_{m=1}^{M}\mathbb{E}\left[y_{m,t}s_{m,t}\right]\geq\alpha, (1b)
∑m=1Mym,t=1,∀t∈{1,…,T},\displaystyle\textstyle\sum\nolimits_{m=1}^{M}y_{m,t}=1,\quad\forall t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}, (1c)
ym,t∈{0,1},∀t∈{1,…,T},m∈{1,…,M},\displaystyle\textstyle y_{m,t}\in\{0,1\},\quad\forall t\in\{1,\ldots,T\},\ m\in\{1,\ldots,M\}, (1d)

where ym,t=1y_{m,t}=1 if model mm serves request tt and 00 otherwise, and sm,t∈{0,1}s_{m,t}\in\{0,1\} denotes whether that response was satisfactory.

Challenges. Our work is primarily motivated by the observation of how users provide feedback in systems like ChatGPT, Claude, or Microsoft Copilot. Users have the option to give a thumbs up or down, whenever they would like to provide feedback. Overall feedback signals are extremely sparse [11, 17]. Since we usually only query one model for a user request, this typically leaves us with one-sided and often imbalanced data, i.e., we do not know the true value of sm,ts_{m,t} for most requests and models. Consequently, we have do deal with unknown performance statistics for all other models that were not queried and did not receive feedback. Furthermore, chat-like requests arrive sequentially in a streaming fashion without the knowledge of statistics of future requests. Hence, we cannot solve problem (1) directly in one shot over the entire time horizon. An online solution that routes the model per request is needed.

2.2 Proposed SLARouter Algorithm

The Lyapunov drift-plus-penalty framework [20] gives a useful starting point for our problem. It operates in an online fashion without requiring knowledge of the underlying request or feedback distribution. It can provide provable guarantees on time-average performance despite unknown future statistics. This stability condition emerges organically from the Lyapunov structure instead being imposed as an ad hoc heuristic. However, the standard framework in [20] as well as its use in [32] still assumes full feedback signals for all the requests. In this work, we present a novel extension to support sparse and imbalanced observations, ensuring that models with insufficient feedback are not perpetually neglected. The overall procedure is in Algorithm 1. We explain the details as follows.

Methodology. SLARouter operates in two phases, exploration and exploitation, controlled by a random process Xt∼Bernoulli​(pt)X_{t}\sim\text{Bernoulli}(p_{t}), where pt=min⁡(1,c/t4)p_{t}=\min\left(1,\nicefrac{{c}}{{\sqrt[4]{t}}}\right) and c∈ℝ+c\in\mathbb{R}^{+}, which is a hyperparameter to control the exploration probability. The exploration probability decays over time, gradually shifting weight toward exploitation as the predictor matures. Central to both phases is a satisfaction predictor, which is a multi-label classifier with one output head per candidate model that independently estimates the probability (denoted by s^m,t\hat{s}_{m,t}) that a given request tt would satisfy a user if served by model mm.

Note, the predictor informs the routing decision but is not responsible for it. The decision is determined by our per-request optimization described below. Once a response was sent to the user, they can provide feedback to indicate whether it was satisfactory or not. As we aim to ensure SLA compliance, we use a virtual queue to capture all violations (negative feedback) over time. The queue length QtQ_{t} affects the routing decision as more violations will pressure the algorithm to choose a more capable and expensive model, and vice versa.

Feedback Availability. Whenever a request is sent to an LLM, the system may or may not receive user feedback about whether the response is satisfactory. This same principle applies to both the exploration and exploitation phases. We do not distinguish between true user feedback and feedback obtained from a separate LLM judge in this section. The performance difference between using user vs. LLM-judge feedback will be studied in the experiments later. If feedback is unavailable (from either the user or the LLM judge) for request tt and model mm, we write sm,t=∅s_{m,t}=\emptyset.

Predictor. The predictor (with trainable parameter vector 𝐳\mathbf{z}) must handle the key structural difficulty of missing labels across heads, which arises from the feedback stream since only the explored model receives a label at each step. Its architecture is illustrated in Figure 1. The overall objective of predictor training is a standard binary cross-entropy loss:

F⁡(𝐳):=−𝔼𝐚t∼𝒜​[1M​∑m=1M(sm,t​log⁡s^​(𝐳,𝐚t)m+(−sm,t)​log⁡(−s^​(𝐳,𝐚t)m))]+μ2​‖𝐳‖2,\displaystyle\textstyle F(\mathbf{z}):=-\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{a}_{t}\sim\mathcal{A}}\left[\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\left(s_{m,t}\log\hat{s}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{a}_{t})_{m}+(1\!-\!s_{m,t})\log(1\!-\!\hat{s}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{a}_{t})_{m})\right)\right]\!+\!\frac{\mu}{2}\left\|\mathbf{z}\right\|^{2}, (2)

where μ>0\mu>0 is a weight-decay coefficient, 𝐚t\mathbf{a}_{t} is the input of the tt-th request, and s^​(𝐳,𝐚t)m=s^m,t\hat{s}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{a}_{t})_{m}=\hat{s}_{m,t} for predictor parameter 𝐳\mathbf{z} and request input 𝐚t\mathbf{a}_{t}.

The uniqueness of SLARouter’s predictor is that it is trained only using one-sided feedback, i.e., feedback from only a single model that is chosen to serve the user. To facilitate this, all the requests with feedback collected from exploration steps are saved in a predictor training dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D}. In each exploration step, if feedback is collected, this new sample (𝐚t,sm~,t,m~)(\mathbf{a}_{t},s_{\tilde{m},t},\tilde{m}) is added to 𝒟\mathcal{D}, where m~\tilde{m} is the randomly chosen model during exploration; then, a step of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with a mini-batch ℬ\mathcal{B}, sampled from 𝒟\mathcal{D}, is performed to update the predictor’s parameter 𝐳\mathbf{z}. The mini-batch size |ℬ|:=min⁡{|𝒟|;B}|\mathcal{B}|:=\min\{|\mathcal{D}|;B\}, where |⋅||\cdot| denotes the cardinality of the set and BB is the default mini-batch size once |𝒟|≥B|\mathcal{D}|\geq B. We denote the mini-batch gradient by ∇F​(𝐳,ℬ)\nabla F(\mathbf{z},\mathcal{B}), which is computed by

∇F​(𝐳,ℬ)=−∇𝐳[1|ℬ|​∑(𝐚t,sm~,t,m~)∈ℬ(sm~,t​log⁡s^​(𝐳,𝐚t)m~+(−sm~,t)​log⁡(−s^​(𝐳,𝐚t)m~))]+μ​𝐳.\displaystyle\!\!\!\!\!\nabla\!F(\mathbf{z},\mathcal{B})\!=-\nabla_{\!\mathbf{z}}\!\!\left[\textstyle\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{(\mathbf{a}_{t},s_{\tilde{m},t},\tilde{m})\in\mathcal{B}}\left(s_{\tilde{m},t}\log\hat{s}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{a}_{t})_{\tilde{m}}\!+\!(1\!-\!s_{\tilde{m},t})\log(1\!-\!\hat{s}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{a}_{t})_{\tilde{m}})\right)\right]\!+\!\mu\mathbf{z}.\!\!\! (3)

Due to the one-sided feedback, it is possible that some LLMs do not have samples in a mini-batch. In that case, the predictor parameters directly connected to the outputs corresponding to those models are not updated for that specific mini-batch SGD step, because the gradient with respect to those parameters is zero as there is no loss term corresponding to those models in (3).

When the feedback availability follows an IID distribution across requests and models, we can easily see that ∇F​(𝐳,ℬ)\nabla F(\mathbf{z},\mathcal{B}) is an unbiased estimate of the full gradient ∇F​(𝐳)\nabla F(\mathbf{z}). Thus, we have addressed the limited feedback problem by drawing an equivalence between random sampling for SGD, random model selection for exploration, and (random) feedback availability.

Routing Decision. As the predictor improves, routing decisions rely increasingly on its predictions. The predictor scores s^m,t\hat{s}_{m,t} and the virtual queue QtQ_{t} jointly determine the per-request decision problem:

min{ym,t:∀m}V⋅∑m=1M\displaystyle\textstyle\min_{\{y_{m,t}:\forall m\}}\quad V\cdot\textstyle\sum_{m=1}^{M} ym,t​Cm,t+Qt​(α−∑m=1Mym,t​s^m,t),\displaystyle\textstyle y_{m,t}C_{m,t}+Q_{t}\left(\alpha-\textstyle\sum_{m=1}^{M}y_{m,t}\hat{s}_{m,t}\right)\mathrm{,} (4a)
s.t. Constraints (1c), (1d).\displaystyle\textrm{Constraints \eqref{eq:one_model}, \eqref{eq:binary}}\,. (4b)

The update rule for QtQ_{t} is defined in (5) below. Parameter V>0V>0 controls the trade-off between cost efficiency and convergence speed. A smaller VV yields faster SLA compliance at higher initial operating cost, while a larger VV prioritizes cost savings at the expense of slower convergence.

Handling Feedback Sparsity. Updating QtQ_{t} in the standard way requires a feedback signal at every step, but explicit user feedback often arrives at low rates in production systems [11, 17]. When sm~,ts_{\tilde{m},t} is unavailable, we substitute it with the predictor score s^m~,t\hat{s}_{\tilde{m},t} as a proxy. QtQ_{t} evolves as follows:

Qt+1={max⁡{0,Qt+α−sm~,t},if ​sm~,t≠∅max⁡{0,Qt+α−s^m~,t},if ​sm~,t=∅.Q_{t+1}=\begin{cases}\max\{0,Q_{t}+\alpha-s_{\tilde{m},t}\},&\textrm{if }s_{\tilde{m},t}\neq\emptyset\\ \max\{0,Q_{t}+\alpha-\hat{s}_{\tilde{m},t}\},&\textrm{if }s_{\tilde{m},t}=\emptyset\end{cases}. (5)

This substitution keeps our Lyapunov analysis intact, provided that the predictor estimate is sufficiently accurate. This is a condition enforced by the exploration schedule, which guarantees continued predictor improvement and adaptation to the user throughout deployment.

3 Performance Analysis

We present the theoretical performance analysis in this section. The full proofs are in Appendix A.

3.1 Predictor Training

Assumption 1.

3.2 SLA Satisfaction

Assumption 3.

We assume that β​Fmin<13\beta F_{\mathrm{min}}<\frac{1}{3}, and there exists at least one model mm such that Pr{sm,t=1}≥q>α\Pr\{s_{m,t}=1\}\geq q>\alpha and (1−ϕ)​β​Fmin<q−α(1-\phi)\beta F_{\mathrm{min}}<q-\alpha, for some q∈(α,1]q\in(\alpha,1].

This assumption states that the predictor architecture is capable enough so that an optimally trained predictor has a small loss. It also states that there is at least one model for which the satisfaction probability is greater than α\alpha, since otherwise the problem becomes infeasible. The last condition weakens as feedback becomes denser and vanishes entirely in the full-feedback case ϕ=1\phi=1. We also assume that the conditions in Lemmas 1 and 2 hold in the following.

Theorem 1.

Let ρ:=q−α−(1−ϕ)​β​Fmin2>0\rho:=\frac{q-\alpha-(1-\phi)\beta F_{\mathrm{min}}}{2}>0, ψ:=Θ⁡((β⁡(1+σ2)ϕ​ρ​(13−β​Fmin))43)\psi:=\Theta\left(\left(\frac{\beta(1+\sigma^{2})}{\phi\,\rho\left(\frac{1}{3}-\beta F_{\mathrm{min}}\right)}\right)^{\frac{4}{3}}\right), γ:=max⁡{α​ψ; 3​V​ΔC}\gamma:=\max\left\{\alpha\psi;\,3V\Delta_{C}\right\}. For any t≥1t\geq 1, we have these upper bounds on the virtual queue length:

𝔼⁡[Qt]≤γ+𝒪⁡(t)and1t​∑τ=1t𝔼⁡[Qτ]≤𝒪⁡(γ+1/ρ),\displaystyle\textstyle\mathbb{E}\left[Q_{t}\right]\leq\gamma+\mathcal{O}\left(\sqrt{t}\right)\quad\text{and}\quad\frac{1}{t}\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\mathbb{E}\left[Q_{\tau}\right]\leq\mathcal{O}\left(\gamma+\nicefrac{{1}}{{\rho}}\right), (9)

where ΔC:=Cmax−Cmin\Delta_{C}:=C_{\max}-C_{\min}, and CmaxC_{\max} and CminC_{\min} are the maximum and minimum costs, respectively.

The proof of Theorem 1 is based on a unique way of analyzing the terms involving feedback availability and the two variants of queue updates in (5). The feedback probability ϕ\phi appears in the denominator in the definition of ψ\psi (and hence γ\gamma), which verifies that the queue tends to be longer when the feedback rate is low. Based on (5) and Lemma 2, we obtain the following corollary.

Corollary 1.

We have the following upper bound on the time-averaged constraint violation:

α−1T​∑t=1T∑m=1M𝔼⁡[ym,t​sm,t]\displaystyle\!\!\!\textstyle\alpha-\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\mathbb{E}\left[y_{m,t}s_{m,t}\right] ≤𝔼⁡[QT+1]T+(−ϕ)​β​Fmin+𝒪⁡((−ϕ)​β​(+σ2)ϕ​T3/4)\displaystyle\textstyle\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[Q_{T+1}\right]}{T}+(1\!-\!\phi)\beta F_{\mathrm{min}}+\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{(1\!-\!\phi)\beta(1\!+\!\sigma^{2})}{\phi\,T^{\nicefrac{{3}}{{4}}}}\right)
≤𝒪⁡(γT+1T)+(−ϕ)​β​Fmin.\displaystyle\textstyle\leq\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\gamma}{T}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}\right)+(1\!-\!\phi)\beta F_{\mathrm{min}}.\!\!\! (10)

As T→∞T\to\infty, the constraint violation approaches the error floor (1−ϕ)​β​Fmin(1-\phi)\beta F_{\mathrm{min}}. When the predictor is more accurate or the feedback rate is high, the constraint violation becomes less severe. For full feedback with ϕ=1\phi=1, we recover the result in [32]. If full SLA compliance at level α′\alpha^{\prime} is required after a finite number of requests T0T_{0}, one may set α\alpha slightly above α′\alpha^{\prime} such that the upper bound is less than α−α′\alpha-\alpha^{\prime} after T0T_{0} steps.

3.3 Cost Optimality

Theorem 2.

For {ym,t:∀m,t}\{y_{m,t}:\forall m,t\} obtained from the SLARouter algorithm (Algorithm 1), there exists a learning rate schedule {ηk:∀k}\{\eta_{k}:\forall k\} such that

𝔼⁡[1T​∑t=1T∑m=1Mym,t​Cm,t]≤COPT+𝒪⁡(βT4+β​Fmin+1V),\displaystyle\textstyle\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{m=1}^{M}y_{m,t}C_{m,t}\right]\leq C^{\mathrm{OPT}}+\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\beta}{\sqrt[4]{T}}+\beta F_{\mathrm{min}}+\frac{1}{V}\right), (11)

where COPTC^{\mathrm{OPT}} is the optimal solution to (1) obtained from an optimal stationary policy that has full statistical knowledge of requests t∈{1,…,T}t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}.

The proof bounds the drift-plus-penalty expression and incorporates Lemma 2 and Theorem 1. The optimality gap gets smaller as TT is larger, up to the irreducible predictor error β​Fmin\beta F_{\mathrm{min}} and the 1/V\nicefrac{{1}}{{V}} term. The parameter VV governs the trade-off between cost optimality and SLA satisfaction, where a larger VV tightens the optimality gap but slows constraint satisfaction, and vice versa. The residual term β​Fmin\beta F_{\mathrm{min}} reflects the irreducible predictor error. When the predictor is expressive, FminF_{\mathrm{min}} is small.

4 Practical Considerations

Positive-Class Reweighting. In practice, the distribution of user feedback is rarely balanced. Users tend to provide predominantly negative feedback to indicate whenever the LLM does not serve their requests sufficiently well. Without accounting for this potential imbalance, the predictor might converge to a trivial constant predictor in the worst case. To counteract this, we use per-model positive-class weights to upweight sparse positive feedback. For each model mm, we maintain running counts of positive and negative observations across all collected feedback and compute pm=Nm−/Nm+,p_{m}=\nicefrac{{N_{m}^{-}}}{{N_{m}^{+}}}, where Nm+N_{m}^{+} and Nm−N_{m}^{-} denote the number of positive and negative feedback samples for model mm in 𝒟\mathcal{D}. At each SGD step, pmp_{m} is applied as the positive-class weight for the corresponding output in the masked BCE loss over the mini-batch B. This rescales the contribution of the minority class proportionally, ensuring the predictor remains discriminative regardless of label skew.11 1 We note that in our benchmark evaluation we do not observe notable imbalance. However, in production deployments imbalance can be significant, making this correction an important safeguard.

Dynamic Adaptation of VV. The parameter VV controls the trade-off between cost efficiency and convergence speed towards the satisfaction target α\alpha. A small VV prioritizes rapid SLA compliance by routing to expensive models early, and vice versa. From our theoretical analysis, we see that VV depends on the cost spread between largest and smallest model in a zoo, making manual tuning of VV fragile. Instead, we adapt VV with a data-driven mechanism V=(Qmax⋅ε)/Δ​CV=(Q_{\max}\cdot\varepsilon)/\Delta C, where QmaxQ_{\max} is the maximum tolerated queue length, ε>0\varepsilon>0 is a cost-sensitivity parameter, and Δ​C\Delta C is the observed mean cost difference between the cheapest and most expensive model. Intuitively, a wider cost spread yields a smaller VV, lowering the pressure toward cheaper models and allowing for timely SLA convergence. This removes a hard-to-tune hyperparameter and improves the adaptivity of SLARouter. We demonstrate the practical benefit in Section 5.2.

5 Experiments

We underpin our theoretical results by an extensive empirical evaluation across a numerous LLM benchmarks. Our code is available on GitHub22 2 Please reach out for repo access while the preprint is under review. . Details on reproducibility are in the appendix.

5.1 Design

Model Zoo & Benchmarks. We construct our model zoo from the Qwen 3.5 family [33]: two dense models (2B, 9B) and two mixture-of-experts models (35B, 122B). Benchmarks span commonsense reasoning (MMLU, SocialIQa, WinoGrande) [13, 27, 25], scientific knowledge (ARC Challenge, ARC Easy, SciQ, GPQA) [7, 31, 24], mathematical reasoning (GSM8K) [8], reading comprehension (BoolQ, LAMBADA) [6, 22], and agentic tasks (ACPBench) [16].

Predictor. We use SGD, a learning rate of 0.0060.006, a weight decay of 0.010.01, a minibatch size of B=16B=16, and set the exploration probability parameter c=0.1c=0.1 [32], if not specified otherwise.

Service Level Agreement. We define α\alpha per benchmark within the capabilities of the model zoo and set V=0.00001V=0.00001 to ensure timely SLA compliance. We explore data-driven VV (Section 4) with Qmax=30Q_{\mathrm{max}}=30 and ε=0.001\varepsilon=0.001, which is desirable for settings with high user satisfaction requirements.

Objective. We minimize the per-inference energy consumption (MJ) under constraint α\alpha, and report the model call ratio per benchmark to characterize routing behavior.

Observational Data. We set the user feedback rate to 0.20.2 for all experiments. This is primarily to allow for sufficient training data for the CARROT and Causal Router classifiers. Below this rate a fair comparison is not possible. However, we do conduct an ablation study on SLARouter to show its performance under lower feedback rates than 0.20.2.

Baselines. We compare SLARouter against CARROT [28], Causal LLM Routing [30], and MESS+ [32]. In our comparison, we include the offline classifier training costs in the total operating cost. For MESS+, we adopt the same VV and cc settings as what we use for SLARouter.

5.2 Results

SLA Guarantees (α\alpha). SLARouter is the only method that satisfies α\alpha without careful per-benchmark hyperparameter tuning, by maintaining accurate constraint tracking through predictor-estimated queue updates under sparse feedback. MESS+ satisfies α\alpha on 5 out of 11 benchmarks, with failures attributable to feedback sparsity stalling QQ updates under its assumption of complete, balanced signals (Table 2). CARROT and the Causal router are competitive and also satisfy α\alpha, but require careful per-benchmark tuning of μ\mu and λ\lambda to do so. In our experiments, we observe that CARROT and the Causal router both require hyperparameter configurations that strongly prioritize user satisfaction over cost to be able to meet the α\alpha requirement. Further details are available in the appendix.

Cost Efficiency. SLARouter achieves the best cost-quality trade-off. It simultaneously satisfies α\alpha and minimizes operating cost. Among methods that meet α\alpha, SLARouter is 1.25×1.25\times and 2.22×2.22\times cheaper than CARROT and the Causal router, respectively. This is due to the interplay between the predictor and the adaptation of QQ at runtime. MESS+ matches SLARouter on cost but undershoots α\alpha on several benchmarks, confirming that low operating cost alone is insufficient without reliable constraint tracking. The cost advantage is most pronounced on demanding workloads. On ACPBench, SLARouter reduces cost by 1.06×1.06\times relative to CARROT and by over 2.5×2.5\times compared to the Causal router. On easier benchmarks (e.g., ARC Easy), differences are smaller as mid-range models suffice.

Satisfaction Accuracy and Margin. SLARouter achieves the highest post-convergence satisfaction rate among adaptive methods on 7 of 11 benchmarks, with a tighter margin above α\alpha than competitors, confirming that its gains stem from more effective use of available signals rather than conservative routing. Unlike MESS+, whose queue underestimates satisfaction shortfalls under sparse feedback, SLARouter’s virtual queue substitutes predictor estimates to maintain uninterrupted constraint tracking throughout deployment. CARROT and the Causal router are competitive, but their margins are sensitive to the benchmark-specific choice of their cost sensitivity parameter.

Data-Driven Adaptation of Cost-Sensitivity VV. Using data-driven VV eliminates the need for grid search while achieving an overall better SLA convergence speed under relevant cost savings. On challenging tasks like ACPBench and GPQA, the data-driven approach reduces operating cost by 3% and 5%, respectively, while achieving identical α\alpha compliance (Table 3). A detailed comparison against a fine-grained grid search is available in the appendix.

Predictor Quality under Sparse Feedback. Synthetic feedback collected from an LLM-based judge is a well-suited supplement for missing user feedback. When users do not provide feedback, SLARouter falls back to synthetic signals from GPT-5.4 with reasoning enabled, which closely mirrors real user feedback with 94.4% and 87.9% agreement on ACPBench and GPQA, respectively. Our analysis shows that the predictor requires relatively few feedback samples to be able to sufficiently estimate the model fit for an incoming request. Specifically, we observe that SLA violations drop significantly once feedback from as few as 90 and 35 interactions is available for ACPBench and GPQA, respectively. Given the sample size of each benchmark, this is equal to a 5% and 8% feedback rate, respectively. The judge comes with no additional burden on end users (Figure 2). Details on the judge and alignment with ground truth data is in the appendix.

6 Conclusion

We present SLARouter, an online LLM router that extends the Lyapunov drift-plus-penalty framework, making it the first routing method to provide theoretical guarantees for cost optimality at a given user satisfaction rate under sparse, one-sided observational feedback. On average, SLARouter reduces operating costs by up to 2.22× over existing baselines while satisfying SLA constraints without per-benchmark tuning. When user feedback is sparse, an LLM-based judge provides a reliable synthetic supplement, enabling robust predictor updates without additional burden on end users. Our approach assumes constant feedback rates and IID request arrivals, which may not hold in production systems where feedback can arrive in bursts and where requests by individual users may be correlated. Hence, we see priority in addressing non-constant feedback rates, feedback arriving in temporal waves, and the challenge of learning routing policies from negativity-biased feedback in future work.

A.2 Total Expectation Result of Lemma 1

We give a formal proof of the total expectation result of Lemma 1, starting with bounding the expectation of kk.

=∑τ=1tϕ​min⁡(1,cτ4)=∑τ=1c4ϕ+∑τ=c4+1tϕ​cτ4\displaystyle=\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\phi\min\left(1,\frac{c}{\sqrt[4]{\tau}}\right)=\sum^{c^{4}}_{\tau=1}\phi+\sum^{t}_{\tau=c^{4}+1}\frac{\phi c}{\sqrt[4]{\tau}} (A.25)
=c4​ϕ+4​ϕ​c3​(t34−c3)=Θ⁡(ϕ​t34)\displaystyle=c^{4}\phi+\frac{4\phi c}{3}(t^{\frac{3}{4}}-c^{3})=\Theta\left(\phi t^{\frac{3}{4}}\right) (A.26)

This proves the first result.

Considering 1k\frac{1}{k}, we adopt the convention that 1k:=0\frac{1}{k}:=0 when k=0k=0, since no predictor update has occurred in that case and Lemma 1 (which is stated for k≥1k\geq 1) contributes no term. where I​l𝒞{\rm I\kern-1.99997ptl}_{\mathcal{C}} is an indicator function of whether the condition 𝒞\mathcal{C} holds, and λ\lambda is as derived in (A.26) accounting for the feedback probability ϕ\phi.

Appendix B Experimental Details & Additional Results

We provide a ready-to-run code base on GitHub: Please reach out for repo access while the preprint is under review. This section provides additional details to reproduce our results and additional experimental results.

B.1 Environment and Hardware

All experiments were executed in a single Python 3.12 environment managed with uv. A full list of locked dependencies can be found in the code base.

Random seeding. We seed all random generators in our experiment, usually with seeds 42, 1, and 1234, if not specified otherwise. For experiment where we use more than 3 seeds, we use the range [1,n][1,n].

Hardware. We conducted all our experiments on a SLURM cluster equipped with NVIDIA H100 GPUs. To collect the benchmark data, we used 1 GPU for Qwen 3.5 2B, 9B-AWQ, and 35B-AWQ. We used 2 GPUs to run Qwen 3.5 122B-AWQ. Otherwise, all experiments presented in this paper require little GPU memory since the routing models are typically ≪1​B\ll 1\mathrm{B} parameters.

B.2 Dataset

We collect all benchmark data by using EleutherAI’s lm-evaluation-harness. We then merge the logged json outputs into a single parquet file that can be consumed by our code base. The dataset contains the cost for querying all LLMs for a specific request (in Megajoules) as well as the actual model response. The responses are particularly relevant for the experiments with the LLM judge. We measure energy using zeus-ml. Each row in the dataset corresponds to one evaluation example and contains:

  • •

    Identifiers: doc_id, benchmark, input_text, correct_answer

  • •

    Per-model binary outcomes: {model}_solved

  • •

    Per-model energy/latency: {model}_energy_joules, {model}_latency_ms

  • •

    Per-model token counts: {model}_prompt_tokens, {model}_completion_tokens

Model zoo.

We use one model zoo with 4 distinct models, specifically Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B, QuantTrio/Qwen3.5-9B-AWQ, QuantTrio/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-AWQ, and QuantTrio/Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-AWQ. Further characteristics are available in Table 4.

Model performance.

Figure B.1 shows per-model accuracy across all 11 benchmarks. Each group of bars corresponds to one benchmark, with individual bars showing the accuracy of each Qwen 3.5 model.

B.3 Predictor: Architecture and Training Details

Architecture. The satisfaction predictor is a multi-label binary classifier built on top of a frozen ModernBERT encoder (D=768D=768 dimensions). The classification head is a two-layer MLP: Dropout​(p=0.1)→Linear​(D,D)→LayerNorm→ReLU→Dropout​(p=0.1)→Linear​(D,|M|)\texttt{Dropout}(p=0.1)\rightarrow\texttt{Linear}(D,D)\rightarrow\texttt{LayerNorm}\rightarrow\texttt{ReLU}\rightarrow\texttt{Dropout}(p=0.1)\rightarrow\texttt{Linear}(D,|M|), where MM is the number of candidate models. At inference time the model outputs MM logits, one per model head, which are passed through a sigmoid to obtain s^m∈[0,1]M\hat{s}_{m}\in[0,1]^{M}.

Optimizer and training hyperparameters. Only the classifier-head parameters are trained; the encoder remains frozen. Optimization uses SGD with momentum 0.900.90 and weight decay 0.010.01. The default learning rate is η=0.006\eta=0.006 (identified via extensive hyperparameter tuning). Gradients are clipped to a maximum ℓ2\ell_{2}-norm of 1.01.0.

Constant versus diminishing learning rate. Our analysis (Lemma 1) uses the diminishing schedule ηk=min⁡{4/μ⁡(k+1),1/2​L}\eta_{k}=\min\{\nicefrac{{4}}{{\mu(k+1)}},\,\nicefrac{{1}}{{2L}}\}, which is the standard technique for last-iterate convergence to the exact minimizer FminF_{\mathrm{min}}. In practice we found a constant rate already sufficient for good performance, so we use it for simplicity. The only cost is convergence to an 𝒪⁡(η​σ2)\mathcal{O}(\eta\sigma^{2}) neighborhood of FminF_{\mathrm{min}} instead of FminF_{\mathrm{min}} exactly, which inflates the floor β​Fmin\beta F_{\mathrm{min}} by a constant and leaves all guarantees intact (they already carry this floor).

Loss function. Training minimizes a masked binary cross-entropy loss. Because each exploration step reveals feedback for only one model, the label matrix contains NaN for all unobserved heads; the loss back-propagates only through the observed entries.

Minibatch buffer. Training occurs only when the minibatch buffer reaches capacity batch_size=16\texttt{batch\_size}=16. The buffer stores tuples (text,m,satisfaction).(\text{text},m,\text{satisfaction}). We sample minibatches randomly from the buffer for every predictor update. When full, the buffer yields a label matrix of shape (B,M)(B,M) with exactly one label per request. By default a single SGD step is taken per full minibatch (classifier_epochs=1\texttt{classifier\_epochs}=1); setting this >1>1 enables multiple passes.

Default hyperparameters (full list). η=0.006\eta=0.006, momentum=0.90=0.90, weight decay=0.01=0.01, batch size=16=16, dropout=0.1=0.1, queue mode=random=\texttt{random}, explore mode=uniform=\texttt{uniform}, classifier epochs=1=1, lr_schedule=fixed\texttt{lr\_schedule}=\texttt{fixed}.

B.4 Performance Matching Between Baselines and SLARouter

We carefully tune the cost parameters of CARROT and Causal Router to match the performance requirements we set for each benchmarks. For CARROT, we search the range μ∈[0,1]\mu\in[0,1] with increments of 0.05 and for Causal Router we search λ∈[0,0.01]\lambda\in[0,0.01] in increments of 0.0010.001.33 3 Note, our λ\lambda range is significantly different from the original paper as we are using energy consumption in joules while the original paper uses USD per 1M tokens. We match the performance against the SLA requirement α\alpha and pick the configuration that comes closest to α\alpha. In order to ensure there is enough training data available for the baselines, we chose --target-feedback-rate 0.2. To train the CARROT and Causal Router classifiers, we use a separate training dataset that consists of the benchmark trainings splits. We collect the data in the same way per our procedure described above for the actual benchmark datasets. We train the classifiers with the same amount of feedback as what MESS+ and SLARouter see at inference time to ensure fair comparison. Full training scripts are provided in the code base for your reference. The classifier training statistics are provided in Table 5. The detailed parameterization is provided in Table 6.

B.5 Data-Driven Selection of VV

We compare a grid search for an appropriate VV value with our data-driven selection mechanism (Table 7). We note that per our theoretical analysis, we will always reach α\alpha and VV only determines how long it takes for SLARouter to converge. Yet, when choosing VV too large, convergence times may become impractical. This is what can be seen when choosing V>0.0001V>0.0001. These values are one order of magnitude apart from one another, so making an educated guess at VV based on reference benchmarks may yield unnecessary inefficiencies. So, overall our data-driven method increases the cost effectiveness of SLARouter beyond what would be possible with a grid search.

B.6 Judge Feedback Alignment

When user feedback is unavailable, we use an LLM-based judge as a scalable alternative to obtain synthetic feedback signals. Specifically, we prompt GPT-5.4 to assess the input/response pairs, and collect binary (correct/incorrect) judgment scores. We measure the alignment (agreement rate) between the judge’s outputs and ground-truth benchmark labels across two challenging evaluations: GPQA [24], a graduate-level science benchmark requiring domain expertise, and ACPBench [16], a planning benchmark that demands multi-step reasoning. We see that disabling reasoning leads to poor alignment (Table 8) and substantially higher error rates across both benchmarks. This confirms the assumption that the SOTA reasoning-capable LLMs are necessary to reliably replicate the user feedback. In our experiments we use the latter setting with feedback collected from a reasoning-enabled judge. Our prompt template to obtain feedback from the judge is geared towards receiving binary feedback to serve as a plug-and-play substitute for actual user feedback ().
